findings.title: Whole-table baseline dispersion (11 rows) indeterminate but flags a concentrated cluster
findings.description: Across all 11 baseline rows the precision multiplier tau-hat=1.44 (CI [0.20, 2.82]) does not distinguish Table 1 from honest randomisation, but an upper-tail Simes test on the row p-values (p=0.057) flags Age, Weight and Height as unusually similar within the whole table. Whole-table pooling dilutes this concentrated cluster.

consequence.explanation: Motivates the targeted subgroup analysis below; does not by itself establish an anomaly.

adjudication.rationale: The whole-table dispersion result is itself indeterminate (tau-hat CI spans 1), but its own upper-tail Simes signal (p=0.057) points at the same Age/Weight/Height rows already flagged by the CSF test; it adds marginal corroboration to that finding rather than standing as an independent one.

findings.title: Baseline Age, Weight, Height too similar across arms (p=0.006)
findings.description: The recomputed one-way ANOVA p-values for baseline Age, Weight and Height (0.931, 0.991, 0.990) are all far above 0.9, and the Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher test finds this excess similarity survives a conservative correlation adjustment (rho=0.5, similarity p=0.0061). Weight's own SDs (27.1, 28.5, 27.2, 28.6) are independently under-dispersed (variance-dispersion p=0.008). This subgroup was selected after seeing the whole-table dispersion screen flag it, which is a legitimate use of that screen's own recommendation but is not a pre-registered test.

consequence.explanation: If randomisation is compromised, all downstream between-group comparisons (the paper's primary claims) are undermined.

findings.notes: Selection of this 3-row subgroup was informed by the whole-table screen's own recommendation, not chosen blind; the full 7-row anthropometric block (Age, Weight, Height, BMI, Waist, Hip, BFR) is only indeterminate (survives correlation), and the 3-row biochemistry block (FBS, TG, TC) is consistent. Report accordingly as a targeted, not omnibus, signal.

adjudication.rationale: Cross-checked with csf_test (rho=0.5, p=0.0061) and check_variance_dispersion (Weight, p=0.0078); both confirmed as printed. Baseline Age/Weight/Height are far more similar than randomisation predicts, even after adjusting for correlation. Per rule 1, uniform high baseline p-values are the red flag, not reassurance -- consistent with a randomisation or data-integrity problem, but capped at 'suspicious', not proof.

findings.title: Full 11-row baseline table is consistent with random allocation
findings.description: Combining all 11 baseline p-values with Stouffer's method at rho=0.5 gives similarity p=0.189, well within the range expected under honest randomisation.

adjudication.rationale: not addressed by the adjudicator

findings.title: Full anthropometric block (7 rows) indeterminate under correlation adjustment
findings.description: Age, Weight, Height, BMI, Waist, Hip, BFR together look too similar under an independence assumption (p=0.0068) but this does not survive a realistic rho=0.5 correlation adjustment (p=0.1085), so no finding is reported at this grouping.

adjudication.rationale: The 7-row anthropometric block's excess-similarity signal does not survive a realistic rho=0.5 correlation adjustment (p=0.11); it neither adds to nor contradicts the narrower, still-significant Age/Weight/Height finding, so it is dropped rather than reported as its own row.

findings.title: Baseline Weight SDs (27.1, 28.5, 27.2, 28.6) are more uniform than sampling error predicts
findings.description: Only 0.78% of honest draws under the equal-variance null cluster this tightly (max_z-min_z=0.108, p=0.0078). This is the strongest single-row signal in Table 1 and reinforces the Age/Weight/Height CSF finding, though it is capped at suspicious and is a relative screening signal, not proof.

consequence.explanation: Contributes to, but does not on its own establish, a randomisation concern.

adjudication.rationale: Confirmed by re-running check_variance_dispersion (p=0.0078, matches the reported figure exactly). The four baseline Weight SDs are more uniform than sampling error predicts; this corroborates the CSF baseline-similarity finding on the same rows but remains capped at 'suspicious' as a relative screening signal, not proof.

findings.title: Group 3 female percentage (63.4%) does not match 19/30 under any rounding convention
findings.description: 19 of 30 Group 3 participants are female, which is 63.333%; the printed 63.4% falls outside the rounding interval [63.35, 63.50) computed both under round-to-nearest and truncation. The paired male figure (36.6% for 11/30) is internally consistent under truncation, so this looks like an isolated slip rather than a wrong count, and the two figures still sum to exactly 100%.

consequence.explanation: Cosmetic; does not affect any inferential claim.

findings.notes: Male 36.6% for the same group (11/30) is consistent under a truncation convention, which makes a single mistyped digit in the female cell the most likely explanation.

adjudication.rationale: Confirmed by re-running check_count_percent: 19/30=63.33%, printed as 63.4%, just outside the rounding interval [63.35, 63.50). The paired male figure (36.6%) is consistent under truncation and the two figures still sum to 100%, so this reads as an isolated rounding/typo slip rather than a wrong headcount -- an erratum-level issue.

findings.title: Methods says 'independent t-test' for within-subject week-0 comparisons
findings.description: The Statistical methods paragraph names only the independent t-test, but every within-group 'compared with baseline' significance marker (*) in Tables 2 and 3 is necessarily a repeated/paired measurement on the same 30 people over time, not an independent-samples comparison. Applying an independent-samples test to paired data is usually conservative (inflates the SE), so this is unlikely to have manufactured false significance, but it is a methods-reporting inconsistency.
findings.location: Statistical methods and data analysis paragraph vs Tables 2 and 3 footnotes
findings.quote: Significant differences between groups were determined by using an indepen-dent t- test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

anchors.quote: Significant differences between groups were determined by using an indepen-dent t- test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

consequence.explanation: If a paired test was actually used but mislabelled, this is a reporting error; if an independent test truly was used on paired data, results are conservative rather than inflated.

adjudication.rationale: Same independent-t-test-on-repeated-measures design issue already covered by the science analyst's version of this finding.

This design (n=30/arm) would need about 330 total participants for 80% power to detect an effect this size, so it is 11x underpowered -- context for interpreting the claimed significance, not itself an error.

findings.title: Baseline biochemical values disagree between Table 1 and Table 3 across four cells
findings.description: Table 1's baseline (week 0) values for FBS (Groups 3 and 4), TC (Group 2) and TG (Group 4) do not match the identical measurement printed as the Week 0 column of Table 3 -- means and/or SDs differ in every case (e.g. FBS Group 3: 119.9±7.2 vs 119.9±12.2; FBS Group 4: 113.6±12.5 vs 118.6±12.5; TC Group 2: 173.6±16.3 vs 175.6±12.9; TG Group 4: 168.1±18.2 vs 166.1±18.2). This is a plain, verified internal contradiction spanning three variables and three groups, not a single arithmetic slip.
findings.location: Table 1 (baseline biochemical row) vs Table 3, Week 0 column
findings.notes: The anthropometric baseline block (weight, BMI, waist, hip, BFR) is internally consistent between Table 1 and Table 2's Week 0 column, which makes the biochemical mismatch a localized rather than a paper-wide problem, but it means a reader cannot tell which of the two printed baseline values for FBS(G3), FBS(G4), TG(G4) and TC(G2) is the one the reported within-group significance tests actually used.

adjudication.rationale: Four independent model-read cell comparisons describe the same defect: the baseline table and the Week-0 outcome column disagree on values that should be identical. Merged into one pattern finding; each table's own within-table trend stays self-consistent, so this is a data-provenance/reporting problem, not one that overturns a specific claim.
adjudication.title_was: Baseline (week 0) FBS and TC values disagree between Table 1 and Table 3
adjudication.description_was: Table 1 reports baseline FBS as 119.9±7.2 (Group 3) and 113.6±12.5 (Group 4), and baseline TC as 173.6±16.3 (Group 2). Table 3's own Week 0 column, describing the identical baseline measurement in the identical groups, instead prints FBS 119.9±12.2 (Group 3, SD differs), FBS 118.6±12.5 (Group 4, mean differs), and TC 175.6±12.9 (Group 2, both mean and SD differ); TG for Group 4 also differs (168.1 vs 166.1). Four of twelve baseline biochemical cells disagree between the paper's own two tables, while every anthropometric baseline cell (Table 1 vs Table 2 Week 0) matches exactly, so the discrepancy is confined to the biochemical panel.

findings.title: Independent t-test used for within-subject repeated-measures comparisons
findings.description: Methods state significance was determined "by using an independent t-test," a single named procedure. But the overwhelming majority of the significance markers in Tables 2 and 3 are baseline-vs-follow-up comparisons WITHIN the same participants over time (the '*' symbol, defined as "compared with baseline (week 0)"), which are paired/repeated-measures data, not independent samples. No paired t-test, repeated-measures ANOVA, or correction for the dozens of pairwise comparisons (baseline vs 3 follow-ups x 4 groups x 3 tables, plus between-group comparisons at each week) is described anywhere in the paper.
findings.location: Statistical methods and data analysis (Methods) vs Tables 2 and 3 footnotes

anchors.label: Methods, Statistical methods and data analysis
anchors.quote: Significant differences between groups were determined by using an independent t-test. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.

findings.notes: This is the analysis underlying essentially every significant result the paper reports (all within-group time-course claims in the Results, Discussion and Conclusion). Treating repeated measurements on the same participants as independent samples, and running dozens of uncorrected pairwise comparisons, both bias the reported p-values in ways the paper does not acknowledge or control for. Handoff: the tool expert may wish to run multiplicity_report over the full set of reported p<0.05 markers to quantify the uncorrected-comparisons problem.

adjudication.rationale: The Methods name only an independent t-test, but the '*' baseline-vs-follow-up markers in Tables 2 and 3 are necessarily within-subject repeated measures on the same 30 people. This is a genuine design/reporting mismatch, but as the finding itself notes an independent test on paired data is typically conservative (inflates SE), so it is unlikely to have inflated the reported significant effects -- a localized methods-reporting correction rather than a result-altering flaw.

findings.title: Discussion claims 6-8 kg / 2.7-3.0 BMI-point reductions Table 2 doesn't support
findings.description: The Discussion states ACV intake "reduced the body weight by 6-8 kg and BMIs by 2.7-3.0 points." Table 2's own week 0-to-week 12 values give weight reductions of 5.1 kg (Group 1), 7.4 kg (Group 2) and 7.0 kg (Group 3), and BMI reductions of 1.8 (Group 1), 2.9 (Group 2) and 2.8 (Group 3) points. Group 1's weight loss (5.1 kg) falls below the claimed 6-8 kg range, Group 1's BMI loss (1.8) falls well below the claimed 2.7-3.0 range, and no group's BMI loss reaches 3.0.
findings.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning "In Lebanon, the percentage..." vs Table 2, Weight and BMI rows

anchors.label: Discussion
anchors.quote: daily oral intake of ACV for 12 weeks reduced the body weight by 6-8 kg and BMIs by 2.7-3.0 points

adjudication.rationale: The Discussion's claimed 6-8 kg / 2.7-3.0 BMI-point reduction range is not supported by Table 2's own week-0-to-week-12 changes; Group 1 shows only 5.1 kg / 1.8 points, both below the claimed range. This overstates the study's own results and should be corrected in the text, though it does not change the direction of the finding or any abstract-level claim.

findings.title: No dropout, exclusion after enrolment, or CONSORT-style flow is reported over 12 weeks
findings.description: All four groups are reported at n=30 at every timepoint (weeks 0, 4, 8, 12) in Tables 1-3, with venous blood draws and full anthropometric batteries required at each visit over a 12-week trial in adolescents and young adults. No flow diagram, no count of screened/excluded/lost-to-follow-up participants, and no discussion of missing data appears anywhere in the paper. Zero attrition over 12 weeks with repeated blood draws is unusually low and is not addressed as a limitation.

anchors.quote: A total of 120 overweight and obese adolescents and young adults (46 men and 74 women) were enrolled in the study and assigned to either placebo group or experimental groups

findings.notes: check_flow_arithmetic on the single reported stage (120 enrolled = 4x30 arms) reconciles exactly, so there is no arithmetic error here -- the finding is the complete absence of any attrition/exclusion reporting for a 12-week trial with repeated venipuncture, which the rulebook (rule 7) flags as itself notable.

adjudication.rationale: Zero attrition across 120 participants over 12 weeks with repeated venous blood draws is unusually clean and worth flagging per rulebook rule 7, but by itself it is a plausibility concern about reporting completeness, not a demonstrated error; kept at its provisional minor severity and named in the paper summary as part of the broader too-clean pattern.

findings.title: Age range 12-25 pooled as one group without stratification
findings.description: Inclusion criteria admit participants aged 12 to 25, a span covering early adolescence through full adulthood, yet all analyses pool this range within each of the four groups with no age-stratified analysis, no pediatric BMI-for-age percentiles (adult BMI cut-points of 27-34 kg/m2 were used uniformly), and body composition measured with a consumer bioelectrical-impedance device marketed for adult use. The resulting very wide within-group SDs for weight (~27-28 kg on means of ~77-79 kg) and height (~20-22 cm on a mean of ~157 cm) are consistent with this unaddressed age heterogeneity.

anchors.quote: age between 12 and 25 years, BMIs between 27 and 34 kg/m2

findings.notes: Handoff to tool expert: check_sd_range / check_variance_dispersion on Table 1's weight (mean~79, SD~27-28, n=30) and height (mean~157, SD~20-22, n=30) rows against the stated age/BMI inclusion bounds would quantify whether this dispersion is attainable.

adjudication.rationale: A valid design limitation -- pooling ages 12-25 without stratification, using adult BMI cut-points and an adult-marketed bioimpedance device -- but this is a scope/generalisability limitation of an otherwise-described method, not an error in a reported number.

findings.title: Table 3 prints an undefined '#' symbol and a doubled asterisk in two cells
findings.description: Table 3's footnotes define only three symbols (*, dagger, double-dagger), but the Group 2 FBS cells at Week 8 and Week 12 print "115.4±12.6*#*†" and "110.1±12.2*#*†" -- an undefined '#' sandwiched between two asterisks. No other cell in the table carries a repeated or undefined symbol.
findings.location: Table 3, FBS row, Group 2, Week 8 and Week 12

anchors.quote:
*p<0.05; compared with baseline (week 0).
†p<0.05; Compared with group 1 within a specific week.
‡p<0.05; Compared with group 2 within a specific week.

adjudication.rationale: An undefined '#' and doubled asterisk in two Table 3 cells is a self-evident typesetting artifact; no reader would misread the underlying value, and no formal correction is warranted beyond a copyediting note.

adjudication.summary: The most serious concern is that Table 1's baseline Age, Weight and Height are statistically far too similar across the four randomised arms (Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher similarity p=0.006, confirmed on re-run and surviving a conservative rho=0.5 adjustment for these correlated measures), reinforced by Weight's own SDs (27.1/28.5/27.2/28.6) being more uniform than sampling error predicts (p=0.008, also confirmed). This pattern is associated with fabricated or non-randomly-allocated data in the literature, though it remains a statistical improbability rather than proof of manipulation. Independently, Table 1's baseline FBS, TC and TG values for several groups do not match the same measurements printed as Table 3's own Week-0 column -- a plain internal contradiction of supposedly identical data. The Discussion also overstates Table 2's own weight/BMI reductions, and the Methods name only an independent t-test for what are mostly within-subject comparisons. Table 2's internal week-by-week trends, most percentages, and the effect-size/summation checks were internally consistent. A journal would need at minimum a corrigendum reconciling Table 1 against Table 3 and correcting the Discussion's overstated range, plus an editorial query about the baseline-similarity signal and randomisation records. This review did not have access to raw participant-level data and cannot establish whether the discrepancies reflect data fabrication, transcription error, or an unreported protocol detail.

rounding_convention.note: Values that fail the round-half convention but are consistent if the reporter TRUNCATES (SPSS's default, and several journal styles). NOT a finding and never counted as one: a single instance is a house style. The RATE is the signal -- this class of anomaly is commoner in papers with more serious problems, so a high proportion is grounds to look harder, not evidence in itself.

sd_convention.note: Values that fail under the sample (Bessel, n-1) SD but are consistent under the POPULATION (n) SD -- numpy's std default and Excel's STDEVP. NOT a finding and never counted as one: choosing a convention is not fabrication. The RATE is the signal, on the same reasoning as the rounding convention above.

harness_sweep.why: These checks were aimed by the harness, not by the model: every eligible target in the paper's tables was enumerated and checked. That makes their coverage identical from run to run, which the model-aimed checks are not -- two runs of this pipeline on one paper overlapped on 0 of 10 model-aimed targets.
